solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Passed away drinking whisky? That’s sad (10)

indicators.note: one word taking in another, as a drinker takes in a drink

annotation.surface: Someone muses that dying with a whisky in hand would be a sad end.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that whisky is only one example of the class wanted: any spirit would do.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to be dispirited is to have lost heart, which is to be sad.

entries.clue: Doing nothing but working? (8)

blocks.note: idleness, the state of not acting
a two-word phrase for operating, as a machine running is

annotation.surface: A wry dig at someone whose only activity is idleness.
annotation.walkthrough: The same letters split two ways: INACTION as one word is idleness, IN ACTION as two words is its opposite. The question mark admits the split.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are plain meanings: one word gives idleness, the two-word phrase gives being at work, so the clue sets opposites against each other.

entries.clue: Plant that climbs most of mountain (3)

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its last letter

blocks.note: PEAK, a mountain, without its last letter K

annotation.surface: A climbing plant that scrambles up a mountainside.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pairs climbing with a mountain, but the climbing belongs to the plant: peas grow on tendrils up sticks.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: pea plants are climbers, clinging to supports with tendrils.

entries.clue: Libertine drinking gallons, contravening norms (5)

indicators.note: one word taking in another, as a drinker takes in a drink

annotation.surface: A debauched man drinking by the gallon and flouting convention.
annotation.walkthrough: Libertine looks like the definition, and ROUE is one, but the answer is the adjective at the other end: a rogue trader or rogue state breaks the rules.
annotation.definitionFit: The adjectival sense: a rogue trader or rogue state acts outside accepted rules, contravening norms.

entries.clue: Montmartre as one embracing rebellion (7)

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer in its arms

annotation.surface: Montmartre, the Paris hilltop district, pictured as a place that welcomes revolt.
annotation.walkthrough: Montmartre is the Paris hill district, famed for artists and the Commune of 1871, which makes the talk of rebellion plausible.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: treason is betrayal of one's state, and rising against it is one form.

entries.clue: Clearly an order Thomas failed to obey? (9)

annotation.definition2: an order Thomas failed to obey

blocks.note: an adverb meaning certainly, without question

blocks.clueFragment: an order Thomas failed to obey
blocks.note: an imperative to be less sceptical, which the apostle Thomas ignored

annotation.surface: A reference to the apostle Thomas, who would not believe in the Resurrection without seeing.
annotation.walkthrough: Doubting Thomas refused to believe until he saw the wounds, so the command 'doubt less' is one he did not follow.
annotation.definitionFit: Clearly is a plain synonym; the second half is a cryptic reading of the same letters as a two-word command.

entries.clue: Trial at first prolonging time in Washington DC (4)

indicators.note: at first means at the very start, so the opening letter of the next word

blocks.note: Eastern Standard Time, the time zone of Washington DC

annotation.surface: A court case dragged out in the American capital.
annotation.walkthrough: Trial reads as a court case, but here it means an ordeal or nuisance, as in 'that child is a trial'.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym in the nuisance sense: a pest tries your patience, and so is a trial.

entries.clue: Old duke resigning from directorship abroad (11)

indicators.note: the duke leaves the word, as one resigns from a post
the letters wander off and scatter

annotation.surface: An elderly duke stepping down from a board position overseas.
annotation.walkthrough: Old looks like it describes the duke; it is the definition, standing alone at the front.
annotation.definitionFit: A hyperbolic use: prehistoric is said loosely of anything very old or outdated.

entries.clue: Foam from English river rising, engulfing hospital (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising turns the letters upward
one piece swallows another

blocks.note: the Tees, a river in north-east England
H = hospital, as on road signs

annotation.surface: Froth rising from an English river as it passes a hospital.
annotation.walkthrough: The reversed English river is split open near its end so the hospital sits inside, just before the final letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: water that seethes foams and churns, like a boiling pot.

entries.clue: Managed to stop former Tory leader ranting (8)

annotation.definitionNote: ranting is used as a noun here, the same as harangue

indicators.note: one word plugs another, as a stopper plugs a bottle

annotation.surface: Someone managing to cut short a one-time Conservative leader mid-rant.
annotation.walkthrough: Tory means Conservative in British politics; William Hague led the party after 1997.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun-for-noun synonym: a long, loud, hectoring speech is both a harangue and a ranting.

entries.clue: Odd country club occasion cut short (6)

indicators.note: a word cut short loses its last letter

blocks.note: the United Nations, a club whose members are countries

annotation.surface: A strange evening at a golf club that ended early.
annotation.walkthrough: A country club is a golf-and-tennis venue; read literally, it is a club of countries.
annotation.definitionFit: The number sense: 3 and 7 are not divisible by two, so odd and not even.

entries.clue: Chief quietly plugging stock (6)

indicators.note: one piece fills a gap in another

blocks.note: a stock phrase is a stale one

annotation.surface: A boss discreetly buying up shares.
annotation.walkthrough: Stock reads as shares, but it is the adjective, as in a stock phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjectival sense: rice is the staple food of much of Asia, meaning the main or principal one.

entries.clue: Unrealistic expectation of lunch on easyJet? (3,2,3,3)

blocks.note: the idiom for a hope that will never come true
a pie eaten on a plane is literally in the sky

annotation.surface: A joke that budget-airline passengers should not hope for a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: easyJet is a British budget airline, famously sparing with free food, which sharpens the joke.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom, from an old protest song promising reward only after death; the literal airborne pie is the second reading.

entries.clue: Take one’s place fast and wait (3,5)

blocks.note: to sit is to take one's seat

annotation.surface: An instruction to be seated quickly and keep still.
annotation.walkthrough: Fast looks like speed; it means firmly, as in 'stuck fast'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: you are told to sit tight when you must stay where you are until something happens.

entries.clue: Reporter ignoring Republican, alleged adulterer (2-10)

indicators.note: to ignore someone is to leave them out, so the letter is left out

annotation.surface: A journalist, a Republican and a rumoured affair: a political scandal.
annotation.walkthrough: In an English divorce case, the co-respondent is the person accused of adultery with the spouse.
annotation.definitionFit: A legal term: the co-respondent is the third party named in a divorce petition as the alleged lover.

entries.clue: Descent from great ape not initially preposterous (9)

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of 'not' is used
absurd, so the letters are thrown into disorder

annotation.surface: Someone dismisses as absurd the idea that humans descend from apes.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is the old evolution row; descent here means lineage, not a climb down.
annotation.definitionFit: The lineage sense: someone of French descent has French parentage.

entries.clue: Writer’s second story making one’s blood run cold (8)

blocks.clueFragment: story making one’s blood run cold
blocks.note: a chiller is a horror story

annotation.surface: An author's follow-up is a horror tale.
annotation.walkthrough: Friedrich Schiller was the German poet and playwright who wrote the Ode to Joy.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Friedrich Schiller, German poet and dramatist.

entries.clue: Prey to anxiety over crew sunk in storm (7,5)

indicators.note: letters caught in a storm are tossed about

annotation.surface: A sailor worried sick about a crew lost in a gale.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface plants a shipwreck, which points at the second word of the answer while hiding the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone who has fallen prey to anxiety is informally called a nervous wreck.

entries.clue: Demanding I run round the States? (7)

annotation.surface: Someone boasting about a gruelling jog around America.
annotation.walkthrough: Round is not an instruction to wrap; it is the round letter O.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an onerous duty is burdensome, making heavy demands.

entries.clue: Conk out in river, cut up inside (6)

indicators.note: the cut piece sits in the river
in a down clue, up turns the letters upward
placed within the other piece

blocks.note: the Exe, a river in Devon

annotation.surface: An engine dies on a river trip, leaving someone upset.
annotation.walkthrough: Conk out is British slang for to break down or die.
annotation.definitionFit: Slang to formal: conk out means die or stop working, and to expire is the formal word for dying.

entries.clue: Old coppers in conversation (8)

blocks.note: coppers are low-value copper coins, loose change

annotation.surface: Retired police officers chatting.
annotation.walkthrough: Coppers reads as police; here it is British slang for small copper coins, pennies.
annotation.definitionFit: A synonym: a brief conversation is an exchange of words, often a sharp one.

entries.clue: Spread out in field? (6)

blocks.note: the surface reads a verb, sprawling; the setter means a noun, a spread of food
not scattered across a field but eaten outdoors, in one

annotation.surface: Something sprawled across a field.
annotation.walkthrough: Spread reads as a verb; it is the noun for a laid-out meal, and 'out' means outdoors.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a picnic is a meal laid out on a rug in the open air.

entries.clue: Group of friends have to drop couple in the end (5)

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so these letters are let go
the removal is from the end of the word

blocks.note: a couple = two letters, the final SS dropped

annotation.surface: A group of friends forced to split up a pair in the end.
annotation.walkthrough: Couple means two letters, taken from the end of POSSESS.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang extension: a posse was a sheriff's band of men, and now informally means a gang of friends.

entries.clue: Rest spots lacking parking at back (6)

indicators.note: the word goes without a letter
letters turned back to front

blocks.note: to spot someone is to spy them

annotation.surface: Lay-bys with no parking at the rear.
annotation.walkthrough: Rest spots reads as roadside stops, but rest alone is the definition and spots is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the siesta is the Spanish afternoon nap, one kind of rest.

entries.clue: Careless constable ignoring new complication (8)

indicators.note: carelessly handled letters get jumbled
to ignore something is to leave it out, so the letter is left out

annotation.surface: A sloppy policeman who overlooks a new difficulty.
annotation.walkthrough: Careless reads as a description of the constable, but it is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: a complication is a difficulty in your way, which is what an obstacle is.

entries.clue: Assistance for Cockney joiner (3)

indicators.note: a word as a Cockney says it, and Cockney speech drops the initial h

blocks.note: to give a hand is to help

annotation.surface: Help offered to a London carpenter.
annotation.walkthrough: Cockneys, working-class Londoners, famously drop the h. Joiner reads as a carpenter; here it is a conjunction joining words.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: a conjunction joins words and clauses, so it is a joiner.

entries.clue: Repudiate last of clergy on retreat (4)

indicators.note: the last of anything is its final part, here the final letter
placed after, in an across clue

blocks.note: a den is a private retreat

annotation.surface: Rejecting the last of the clergy on a religious retreat.
annotation.walkthrough: Retreat reads as a religious retreat, fitting the clergy; it is a den.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to repudiate a claim is to reject it as untrue.

entries.clue: Ed sneers at silly show (10)

indicators.note: the letters behave foolishly and get rearranged

annotation.surface: A man called Ed mocking a silly TV programme.
annotation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a long-running BBC soap opera set in east London.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the BBC soap opera is one television show.
